look_here_first: Look for the comparatively DENSE panicle: large, many-flowered spikelets packed into clusters along ascending branches. Many can appear rosy-red or violet, but spikelet DENSITY and CLUSTERING are stronger than color. Use a mature isolated spikelet to confirm multiple florets before deciding.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays, Blanco, and Llano — specimen-backed county records in Hagenbuch & Lemke's Texas Hill Country grass treatment.

best_field_traits: leaf blades narrow, flat to involute
spikelets conspicuously clumped along branches and branchlets
spikelets pale green to violet or reddish
branch angle appressed to ascending rather than broadly divergent
morphology_keys.comparison_training: The clustered, reddish spikelets are the fast cue. E. spectabilis has many widely spaced spikelets on flexuous, broadly spreading branches; E. lugens has a more restrained panicle and very narrow involute leaves.
morphology_keys.field_teaching_note: Kew/GrassBase describes secundiflora with spikelets clumped along branches, typically many-flowered, 6–20 mm in broader treatment. The photo labels mark clusters only: there are no counted, measured florets.

comparisons.key_distinctions: E. spectabilis: open flexible cloud with more separate spikelets; E. cilianensis: annual often with conspicuous craterlike glands along branchlets and lemma keels. E. lugens: narrow inrolled leaves and markedly smaller solitary spikelets; Tridens texanus: do not assume genus from reddish panicle, verify grass spikelet floral details.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Red lovegrass — inspect true spikelets and the pictured leaf/sheath junctions
steps: Start with Patrick Alexander's public-domain photograph of mature pink reddish spikelets. The overlapping scales shown belong to flowering spikelets; don't guess floret or vein count from this view.

Use Douglas Goldman's close oxylepis flowering branch and the visually verified arrow pointing to the attached overlapping spikelets. This source specifically describes the oxylepis form, not necessarily all red-lovegrass regional forms.

Examine the two true blade/sheath junction closeups. The arrow points to the blade entering the sheath, not to a separately measured ligule; with a live specimen gently expose the actual inner tongue.
Compare red lovegrass spikelets against the locally archived purple lovegrass (*E. spectabilis*) panicle reference; color and a panicle view alone cannot guarantee a species diagnosis.
To finish the photo proof, collect one vouchered mature spikelet with 1-mm ruler and dissect glumes/lemmas and mature florets; separately expose short true ligule hairs with the same scale.

Verify an actual Hays or regional plant's crown, collar, inflorescence and seed head all belong to the same accession. The present Commons photographs are source-labelled out-of-region teaching references.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Physical species-recognition evidence: reddish compressed many-flowered spikelets + real leaf sheath/collar, with oxylepis qualification on the Goldman macro references; do not substitute appearance for same-specimen microscopy.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: All four new JPEGs public-safe CC0/CC BY-SA 4.0 and physically read back in GitHub. Two gross-structure arrows added only to obvious photographed spikelet cluster and leaf/sheath insertion. No new claim of visible ligule hair fringe, measured spikelet florets, source Hays locality, or completed Pages/mobile QA.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — CLUSTERED SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Perennial bunchgrass with chunky multi-flowered spikelets grouped on ascending branches.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow a whole panicle, not just the red color. GrassBase describes panicles ~5–30 cm long, sometimes contracted, with spikelets CLUMPED along branches and short ~0.5–1 mm pedicels. Real Patrick Alexander and Douglas Goldman photographs show flowering clusters; Goldman closeups are source-labelled subsp. oxylepis, not proof of all varieties. Existing gallery panels 0–1 are real mature spikelet clusters; panel 4 is another cluster photograph. Panel 5 is a separate provisionally determined sparse view and should not be treated as verified dense red-lovegrass architecture.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE-LABELLED MATURE CLUSTERS AVAILABLE — FORM AND MEASUREMENT HOLD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED PERENNIAL + SHEATH
field_id_short_tiles.short: Perennial tuft, flowering culms commonly ~30–75 cm; blades ~2–2.5 mm wide in GrassBase.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Confirm a persistent rooted crown and connected flowering culm. Do not decide perennial versus annual from a detached panicle. GrassBase reports flat or inrolled narrow blades and hairy sheath mouth; these are literature-based dimensions, not measurements from archived gallery pixels. Existing Texas in-soil habit panels 6 (Seadrift) and 7 (Willow Park) show living lower bunches and attached flowering culms, but no exposed fibrous roots or rhizomes. Panels 2–3 and 8 instead show exterior blade–sheath junctions, not roots.
field_id_short_tiles.status: IN-SOIL TEXAS BUNCH AND FLOWERING CULMS AVAILABLE — EXPOSED ROOTS STILL NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · TRUE LIGULE VERSUS SHEATH-MOUTH HAIRS
field_id_short_tiles.short: TRUE ligule is a short fringe of hairs; do not invent a millimeter value.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Pull the blade away from its sheath and inspect the inner junction at 10–20×. Distinguish actual ligule hairs from the longer outer oral/collar hairs. The existing two Goldman subsp. oxylepis images show the leaf insertion, but NOT a reliably unfolded and measured true fringe; their arrows must not be relabeled 'ligule' without pixel proof. Panel 8 adds a source-identified exterior blade/sheath V from Texas, not an opened free ligule; panels 2–3 remain explicitly subsp. oxylepis. Do not transfer oxylepis-only visual details to all forms.
field_id_short_tiles.status: THREE EXTERIOR COLLAR VIEWS AVAILABLE — FREE INNER LIGULE STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE MATURE SPIKELETS
field_id_short_tiles.details: On one source-vouchered ripe spikelet, photograph both faces with 1-mm scale, count actual stacked florets, and distinguish each floret from the whole spikelet. GrassBase describes disarticulation below individual florets. The existing mature pink-red cluster photos establish gross arrangement, not a reliable measured floret count. Existing panels 0–1 and 4 demonstrate mature stacked florets and clusters without an independent 1-mm calibration; do not re-request another generic clustered flowering head.
field_id_short_tiles.status: MATURE SPIKELET CLUSTERS AVAILABLE — CALIBRATED FLORET COUNT MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · TWO GLUMES, LEMMA, PALEA AND AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower glume ~2.5–3 mm (1 vein), upper ~3–4 mm (1 vein); fertile lemma ~1.6–2.4 mm (3 veins), NO long awn.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Dissect one mature spikelet at 20–40×: both membranous basal glumes are shorter than the spikelet; the lower is ~70–80% the upper. Separate a three-veined red-to-brown fertile lemma and its palea (palea keels may be ciliate). GrassBase describes acute lemma apex, not a long projecting awn. These are published ranges, not proof of microscopic details in the archived photos.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES + PUBLIC-READY GATE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Red color is not enough: compare purple lovegrass, stinkgrass, plains lovegrass and Tridens.
field_id_short_tiles.details: E. spectabilis has widely spreading flexible branches with more dispersed spikelets; E. cilianensis is an introduced ANNUAL with coarser often gland-pitted structures; E. lugens has narrower rolled blades and smaller dispersed spikelets; Tridens texanus may be rosy but has distinct three-veined lemma anatomy. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: a Texas-vouchered specimen exposing true roots (existing panels 6–7 show in-soil habit), unfolded measured true inner hair-fringe ligule (panels 2–3,8 are exterior junctions), and 1-mm mature spikelet dissection with both glumes, lemma and palea; a same-scale E. spectabilis comparison (existing panel 9 is unscaled).
